abstract.text: The Planckian relaxation rate ~/tP = 2πkBT sets a characteristic timescale for both the equilibration of quantum critical systems and maximal quantum chaos. In this note, we show that at the critical coupling between a superconducting dot and the complex Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model, known to be maximally chaotic, the pairing gap ∆ behaves as η ~/tP at low temperatures, where η is an order one constant. The lower critical temperature emerges with a further increase of the coupling strength so that the finite ∆ domain is settled between the two critical temperatures.

thesis.text: At the critical coupling between a superconducting quantum dot and the complex SYK model, the low-temperature pairing gap is proportional to the Planckian relaxation rate, producing a reentrant superconducting phase between two critical temperatures.

citations.context: The paper opens by positioning its result relative to conventional BCS theory and strange metals, then builds the model.
The paper first motivates the model with Planckian relaxation, SYK/cSYK, and strange-metal phenomenology.
It then defines the superconducting dot, SYK bath, tunneling, and saddle-point equations.
The normal phase, critical coupling, and reentrant superconductivity are developed next.
The Planckian gap result is supported numerically and analytically, with comparison to Andreev billiards.
The conclusion suggests OTOC and cSYK quantum-dot applications.
Appendices derive the gap equation and describe the numerical adaptive golden-ratio method.

references.title: The equilibration time and the Lyapunov time are a priori different physical quantities. Nevertheless, the fact that both quantities are subjected to the same bound raises the question of whether those two seemingly independent quantities might be related. This hypothesis has been intensively investigated in the context of the AdS/CFT correspondence, in large–N vector models and spin systems (see [65] and the references therein). In systems with a small parameter (large–N quantum field theories or weakly coupled field theories) where a regime of exponential growth is present in the OTOC, however, they are set by the same physics even though they are quantitatively different [66,67].
